chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter X
paragraphs: On August 30, Pierre reached Moscow. Near the city gates he was met by Count Rostopchin's adjutant.
"We've been looking for you everywhere," said the adjutant. "The count wants to see you urgently. He asks you to come at once on a very important matter."
Without going home, Pierre took a cab and drove to see the Moscow commander in chief.

Count Rostopchin had returned to town from his summer villa at Sokolniki only that morning. The anteroom and reception room of his house were full of officials who had been summoned or had come for instructions. Vasilchikov and Platov had already met with the count and explained that it was impossible to defend Moscow — it would have to be surrendered. Though this news was being kept from the residents, the officials — the heads of the various government departments — knew that Moscow would soon fall to the enemy, just as Rostopchin himself knew it. To avoid personal responsibility, they had all come to the governor to ask how to handle their departments.
As Pierre was entering the reception room, a courier from the army came out of Rostopchin's private room.
In answer to the questions people fired at him, the courier made a despairing gesture with his hand and passed through the room.

While waiting in the reception room, Pierre watched the various officials — old and young, military and civilian — with weary eyes. They all seemed dissatisfied and uneasy. Pierre approached a group of men, one of whom he knew. After greeting Pierre, they continued their conversation.
"If they're sent away and brought back later, no harm done — but as things stand now, nobody can guarantee anything."
"But look at what he writes..." said another, pointing to a printed sheet in his hand.
"That's a different matter. That's meant for the people," said the first.
"What is it?" asked Pierre.
"Oh, another broadsheet."
Pierre took it and began reading.

His Serene Highness has passed through Mozhaysk to join up with the troops moving toward him and has taken up a strong position where the enemy won't attack soon. Forty-eight guns with ammunition have been sent to him from here, and his Serene Highness says he will defend Moscow to the last drop of blood and is even prepared to fight in the streets. Don't worry, brothers — the courts are closed because things need to be put in order, and we'll deal with the criminals our own way! When the time comes I'll call for both townsmen and peasant lads, and I'll raise the cry a day or two beforehand — but they're not needed yet, so I'm holding my tongue. An ax will do nicely, a hunting spear isn't bad, but a three-pronged pitchfork is best of all: a Frenchman is no heavier than a sheaf of rye. Tomorrow after dinner I'll take the Iberian icon of the Mother of God to the wounded at the Catherine Hospital, where we'll bless some water. That will help them get well quicker. I'm well now too — one eye was sore but now I'm keeping watch with both.
"But military men have told me it's impossible to fight in the city," said Pierre, "and that the position..."
"Of course! That's exactly what we were saying," replied the first speaker.
"And what does he mean by 'One eye was sore but now I'm watching with both'?" asked Pierre.

"The count had a sty," the adjutant replied, smiling, "and was very upset when I told him people had been asking what was wrong with him. By the way, Count," he added suddenly, turning to Pierre with a smile, "we hear you have family troubles — that the countess, your wife..."
"I haven't heard anything," Pierre replied indifferently. "But what have you heard?"
"Oh, well, you know how people invent things. I'm only saying what I heard."
"But what did you hear?"
"Well, they say," the adjutant continued with the same smile, "that the countess, your wife, is preparing to go abroad. I'm sure it's nonsense..."
"Possibly," Pierre remarked, looking around absently. "And who is that?" he asked, indicating a short old man in a clean blue peasant coat, with a big snow-white beard and eyebrows and a ruddy face.
"Him? That's a tradesman — the restaurant keeper, Vereshchagin. Maybe you've heard about that business with the proclamation."
"Oh, so that's Vereshchagin!" said Pierre, studying the firm, calm face of the old man and looking for any sign that he might be a traitor.
"That's not the man himself — that's the father of the one who wrote the proclamation," said the adjutant. "The young man is in prison, and I expect things will go badly for him."
An old gentleman wearing a decoration and another official, a German with a cross around his neck, approached the speaker.

"It's a complicated story, you know," said the adjutant. "That proclamation appeared about two months ago. The count was informed and ordered an investigation. Gabriel Ivanovich here made the inquiries. The proclamation had passed through exactly sixty-three hands. He'd ask one person, 'Where did you get it?' — 'From so-and-so.' He'd go to the next — 'Where did you get it?' — and so on until he reached Vereshchagin, a half-educated tradesman, 'a pet of a merchant,' as they say." The adjutant smiled. "They asked him, 'Who gave it to you?' Now the point is, we knew who'd given it to him. He could only have gotten it from the Postmaster. But evidently they'd made some arrangement. He answered: 'From nobody — I wrote it myself.' They threatened and questioned him, but he stuck to his story: 'I wrote it myself.' And so it was reported to the count, who sent for the man. 'Where did you get the proclamation?' — 'I wrote it myself.' Well, you know the count," the adjutant said cheerfully, smiling with pride, "he flew into a terrible rage — just imagine the man's audacity, lying and stubbornness!"
"And the count wanted him to say it came from Klyucharev? I see!" said Pierre.

"Not at all!" the adjutant replied in dismay. "Klyucharev had his own sins to answer for, which is why he was banished. But the point is, the count was furious. 'How could you have written it yourself?' he said, and he grabbed the Hamburg Gazette lying on the table. 'Here it is! You didn't write it — you translated it, and translated it wretchedly, because you don't even know French, you fool!' And what do you think? 'No,' says the man, 'I haven't read any newspapers — I made it up myself.' 'If that's so, you're a traitor and I'll have you tried and hanged! Tell me who gave it to you.' 'I haven't seen any papers — I made it up myself.' And that was the end of it. The count had the father brought in, but the son stuck to his story. He was sent to trial and sentenced to hard labor, I believe. Now the father has come to plead for him. But he's a worthless fellow! You know the type — a tradesman's son, a dandy and ladies' man. He attended some lectures somewhere and thinks the devil himself is no match for him. That's the kind of fellow he is. His father runs a cookshop here by the Stone Bridge, and you know there was a large icon of God Almighty painted with a scepter in one hand and an orb in the other. Well, he took that icon home for a few days, and what did he do? He found some scoundrel of a painter..."

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XI
paragraphs: In the middle of this story Pierre was summoned to the commander in chief.

When he entered the private room, Count Rostopchin — his face scrunched up — was rubbing his forehead and eyes with his hand. A short man was saying something, but when Pierre came in, he stopped and left.

"Ah, hello there, great warrior!" said Rostopchin as soon as the short man had gone. "We've heard about your heroics. But that's not why you're here. Between us, my friend — are you a Mason?" He went on sternly, as though there were something wrong with it that he nevertheless intended to overlook. Pierre said nothing. "I am well informed, my friend, but I know there are Masons and Masons, and I hope you are not one of those who, under the pretense of saving mankind, wish to ruin Russia."
"Yes, I am a Mason," Pierre replied.

"There, you see, my friend! I expect you know that Messrs. Speransky and Magnitsky have been sent where they belong. Mr. Klyucharev has been treated the same way, and so have others who, under the guise of building Solomon's Temple, have tried to destroy the temple of their fatherland. You can understand there are reasons for this, and I could not have exiled the Postmaster had he not been a dangerous man. It has now come to my knowledge that you lent him your carriage for his departure from the city, and that you even took papers from him for safekeeping. I like you and don't wish you any harm, and since you're only half my age, I advise you as a father would: cut off all contact with people of that kind and leave here as soon as possible."
"But what did Klyucharev do wrong, Count?" asked Pierre.
"That is for me to know, not for you to ask!" Rostopchin shouted.
"If he is accused of distributing Napoleon's proclamation, it hasn't been proved," said Pierre, not looking at Rostopchin, "and Vereshchagin..."

"There we are!" Rostopchin shouted at Pierre even louder than before, scowling. "Vereshchagin is a renegade and a traitor who will be punished as he deserves," he said with the vindictive heat people show when recalling an insult. "But I didn't summon you to discuss my actions. I summoned you to give you advice — or an order, if you prefer. I ask you to leave the city and sever all ties with people like Klyucharev. And I'll knock the nonsense out of anyone" — but probably realizing he was shouting at Bezukhov, who so far wasn't guilty of anything, he added, taking Pierre's hand in a friendly way — "We're on the eve of a public catastrophe and I haven't time to be polite to everyone who has business with me. My head is spinning sometimes. Well, my friend, what are you doing personally?"
"Nothing," answered Pierre, without raising his eyes or changing his thoughtful expression.
The count frowned.

"A word of friendly advice, my friend: get out of here as soon as you can — that's all I have to say. A word to the wise. Goodbye, my dear fellow. Oh, by the way!" he shouted through the doorway after Pierre. "Is it true that the countess has fallen into the clutches of the Jesuits?"
Pierre did not answer and left Rostopchin's room more sullen and angry than he had ever shown himself.

When he reached home it was already getting dark. About eight people had come to see him that evening: the secretary of a committee, the colonel of his battalion, his steward, his major-domo, and various petitioners. They all had business with Pierre and needed decisions. Pierre didn't understand any of their questions and wasn't interested in them; he answered only to get rid of these people. When finally left alone, he opened and read his wife's letter.

"They — the soldiers at the battery, Prince Andrew killed... that old man... Simplicity is submission to God. Suffering is necessary... the meaning of everything... one must harness... my wife is getting married... One must forget and understand..." And going to his bed he threw himself on it without undressing and instantly fell asleep.

When he woke the next morning, the major-domo came to tell him that a special messenger — a police officer — had come from Count Rostopchin to find out whether Count Bezukhov had left or was leaving the city.
A dozen people with business were waiting for Pierre in the drawing room. He dressed hurriedly and, instead of going to see them, went to the back porch and out through the gate.
From that time until the end of Moscow's destruction, none of the Bezukhov household — despite all their searching — saw Pierre again or knew where he was.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XII
paragraphs: The Rostovs remained in Moscow until September 1 — the eve of the enemy's entry into the city.

After Petya had joined Obolensky's Cossack regiment and left for Belaya Tserkov where the regiment was forming, the countess was seized with terror. The thought that both her sons were at war — that both had left the safety of her wing, and that today or tomorrow either or both might be killed, as the three sons of one of her acquaintances had been — struck her that summer for the first time with cruel clarity. She tried to get Nicholas sent home and wanted to go herself to fetch Petya, or to get him assigned somewhere in Petersburg, but neither proved possible. Petya couldn't return unless his regiment did, or unless he was transferred to another active unit. Nicholas was somewhere with the army and hadn't written since his last letter, which gave a detailed account of his meeting with Princess Mary. The countess couldn't sleep at night, and when she did she dreamed of her sons lying dead. After many consultations, the count devised a way to calm her: he got Petya transferred from Obolensky's regiment to Bezukhov's, which was training near Moscow. Though Petya would remain in service, this transfer gave the countess the consolation of having at least one son within reach, and she hoped to arrange things so he'd never be sent to battle again. As long as only Nicholas was in danger, the countess imagined she loved her firstborn more than all her other children and even reproached herself for it; but when her youngest — the scapegrace who'd been bad at lessons, always breaking things and annoying everyone, that snub-nosed Petya with his cheerful black eyes and fresh rosy cheeks where soft fuzz was just beginning to show — when he was thrown among those big, terrible, cruel men who were fighting somewhere about something and apparently enjoying it, then his mother felt she loved him more, much more, than all the rest. The nearer the time came for Petya to return, the more anxious the countess grew. She began to think she would never live to see such happiness. The presence of Sonya, of beloved Natasha, or even of her husband irritated her. "What do I need them for? I need no one but Petya," she thought.

At the end of August the Rostovs received another letter from Nicholas. He wrote from the province of Voronezh, where he'd been sent to procure horses, but the letter did not ease the countess. Knowing one son was out of danger only made her more anxious about Petya.

Although by the twentieth of August nearly all the Rostovs' acquaintances had left Moscow, and everyone urged the countess to leave as quickly as possible, she refused to hear of going before her treasure — her adored Petya — returned. On August 28 he arrived. The passionate tenderness with which his mother received him displeased the sixteen-year-old officer. Though she hid from him her plan to keep him close, Petya guessed her intentions and, instinctively fearing that he might give in to emotion with her — might "go soft," as he put it to himself — he treated her coolly, avoided her, and during his stay in Moscow attached himself exclusively to Natasha, for whom he had always had an especially brotherly, almost lover-like tenderness.

Due to the count's habitual carelessness, nothing was ready for departure by August 28, and the carts that were supposed to come from their Ryazan and Moscow estates to carry away their belongings didn't arrive until the thirtieth.

From the twenty-eighth to the thirty-first, all Moscow was in an uproar. Every day thousands of men wounded at Borodino were brought in through the Dorogomilov gate and taken to various parts of the city, and thousands of carts carried residents and their possessions out through the other gates. Despite Rostopchin's broadsheets — or because of them, or independently of them — the wildest and most contradictory rumors circulated. Some said no one would be allowed to leave; others said all the icons had been removed from the churches and everyone would be ordered to go. Some claimed another battle after Borodino had routed the French, while others insisted the Russian army had been destroyed. Some talked about the Moscow militia marching to the Three Hills led by the clergy; others whispered that Father Augustin had been forbidden to leave, that traitors had been caught, that peasants were rioting and robbing people on the roads out of Moscow, and so on. But all this was only talk; in reality — though the Council of Fili, at which it was decided to abandon Moscow, had not yet been held — both those who left and those who stayed felt, though they didn't show it, that Moscow would certainly be given up and that they should get away as quickly as possible. Everyone sensed that everything would suddenly collapse and change, but through September 1 nothing had. Like a condemned man being led to execution who looks around and straightens the crooked cap on his head, Moscow involuntarily continued its usual life, though it knew the time of its destruction was near — when the conditions its people were accustomed to would be completely overturned.

During the three days before the occupation, the entire Rostov family was absorbed in various activities. The head of the family, Count Ilya Rostov, drove about the city constantly, collecting rumors from all sides and issuing hasty, confused orders at home about preparations for departure.

The countess watched the packing, was dissatisfied with everything, was constantly chasing after Petya — who kept running away from her — and was jealous of Natasha, with whom he spent all his time. Sonya alone handled the practical side, getting things packed. But lately Sonya had been particularly sad and quiet. Nicholas's letter, in which he mentioned Princess Mary, had prompted joyful comments from the countess — made in Sonya's presence — about seeing Providence at work in bringing the princess and Nicholas together.

"I was never pleased about Bolkonsky's engagement to Natasha," said the countess, "but I always wanted Nicholas to marry the princess, and had a feeling it would happen. What a good match it would be!"

Sonya felt this was true — that the only way to restore the Rostov family's finances was for Nicholas to marry a wealthy woman, and that the princess was an excellent match. It was very bitter for her. But despite her grief — or perhaps because of it — she took on all the difficult work of organizing the packing and was busy all day long. The count and countess turned to her whenever orders needed giving. Petya and Natasha, by contrast, were generally a nuisance and a hindrance. Nearly all day the house rang with their running feet, their shouts, and their spontaneous laughter. They laughed and were joyful not because there was any reason to be, but because gladness and mirth filled their hearts and so everything that happened gave them cause for laughter. Petya was in high spirits because having left home a boy he had returned — as everyone told him — a fine young man; because he was at home; because he'd left Belaya Tserkov where there was no hope of seeing battle anytime soon and had come to Moscow where there would be fighting any day; and chiefly because Natasha, whose lead he always followed, was in high spirits. Natasha was gay because she had been sad too long and now nothing reminded her of the cause of her sadness, and because she was feeling well. She was also happy because she had someone to adore her — the adoration of others was the lubricant her machinery needed to run smoothly, and Petya adored her. Above all, they were gay because there was a war near Moscow, there would be fighting at the city gates, weapons were being handed out, everyone was escaping and going somewhere, and in general something extraordinary was happening — and that is always exciting, especially to the young.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XIII
paragraphs: On Saturday, August 31, everything in the Rostov house seemed topsy-turvy. All the doors were open, all the furniture was being carried out or rearranged, and the mirrors and pictures had been taken down. Trunks stood in the rooms, and hay, wrapping paper, and rope were scattered about. The peasants and house servants carrying things out trod heavily on the parquet floors. The yard was crowded with peasant carts — some loaded high and already roped up, others still empty.

The voices and footsteps of the many servants and the peasants who'd come with the carts echoed through the yard and house as they shouted to one another. The count had been out since morning. The countess, with a headache from all the noise and chaos, lay in the new sitting room with a vinegar compress on her forehead. Petya wasn't home — he'd gone to see a friend about getting a transfer from the militia to the active army. Sonya was in the ballroom overseeing the packing of glassware and china. Natasha sat on the floor of her dismantled room amid scattered dresses, ribbons, and scarves, staring at the floor and holding in her hands the old ball gown — already out of fashion — that she'd worn to her first Petersburg ball.

Natasha was ashamed of doing nothing when everyone else was so busy. Several times that morning she'd tried to help, but her heart wasn't in it, and she simply didn't know how to do anything without giving it her whole heart and soul. For a while she'd stood beside Sonya while the china was being packed and tried to assist, but soon gave up and went to her room to pack her own things. At first she enjoyed giving away dresses and ribbons to the maids, but when that was done and what remained still had to be packed, she found it tedious.

"Dunyasha, you pack it! You will, won't you, dear?" And when Dunyasha cheerfully promised to do it all, Natasha sat down on the floor, took her old ball gown, and drifted into a daydream entirely unrelated to what should have occupied her thoughts. She was roused by the chatter of the maids in the next room and their hurried footsteps toward the back porch. Natasha got up and looked out the window. An enormously long row of carts full of wounded men had stopped in the street.
The housekeeper, the old nurse, the cooks, coachmen, maids, footmen, postilions, and kitchen boys all stood at the gate, staring at the wounded.
Natasha, throwing a clean handkerchief over her hair and holding an end in each hand, went out into the street.

The former housekeeper, old Mavra Kuzminichna, had stepped out from the crowd at the gate and approached a cart with a hood made of bark matting. She was talking to a pale young officer who lay inside. Natasha came a few steps closer and stopped shyly, still holding her handkerchief, listening to what the housekeeper was saying.
"So you have nobody in Moscow?" she was saying. "You'd be more comfortable in a house somewhere — in ours, for instance. The family is leaving."
"I don't know if it would be allowed," the officer replied weakly. "There's our commanding officer — ask him," and he pointed to a stout major walking back along the street past the line of carts.
Natasha glanced with frightened eyes at the wounded officer's face and immediately went to meet the major.
"May the wounded men stay in our house?" she asked.
The major raised his hand to his cap with a smile.
"Which one would you like, miss?" he said, squinting and smiling.

Natasha quietly repeated her question, and her face and whole manner were so serious — though she was still holding the ends of her handkerchief — that the major stopped smiling and, after a moment's reflection, as if weighing whether it could be arranged, answered in the affirmative.
"Oh yes, why not? They may," he said.
With a slight nod, Natasha hurried back to Mavra Kuzminichna, who was still talking sympathetically to the officer.
"They may! He says they may!" she whispered.

The cart carrying the officer was turned into the Rostovs' yard, and at the invitation of the townspeople, dozens of carts with wounded men began pulling into the yards and drawing up at the entrances of houses along Povarskaya Street. Natasha was clearly pleased to be dealing with new people outside her ordinary routine. She and Mavra Kuzminichna tried to get as many wounded as possible into their yard.
"Your papa should be told, though," said Mavra Kuzminichna.
"Never mind, never mind — what does it matter? For one day we can move into the drawing room. They can have our whole half of the house."
"Really now, young lady, the ideas you get! Even if we put them in the wing — the men's room or the nurse's room — we still need permission."
"Well, I'll ask."
Natasha ran into the house and went on tiptoe through the half-open door into the sitting room, where there was a smell of vinegar and Hoffmann's drops.
"Are you asleep, Mama?"
"What sleep?" said the countess, waking up just as she was drifting off.

"Mama, darling!" said Natasha, kneeling by her mother and bringing her face close. "I'm sorry — forgive me — I'll never do it again. I woke you up! Mavra Kuzminichna sent me — they've brought wounded men here, officers. Will you let them stay? They have nowhere to go. I knew you'd say yes!" she said all in one breath.
"What officers? Who's been brought? I don't understand anything," said the countess.
Natasha laughed, and the countess smiled slightly too.
"I knew you'd give permission — so I'll tell them," and, kissing her mother, Natasha jumped up and went to the door.
In the hall she met her father, who had returned with bad news.
"We've stayed too long!" the count said with involuntary irritation. "The Club is closed and the police are leaving."
"Papa, is it all right? I've invited some of the wounded into our house," said Natasha.
"Of course, of course," he answered absently. "That's not the point. Please stop fussing with trifles and help with the packing. Tomorrow we must go — go, go!"
And the count gave similar orders to the major-domo and servants.

At dinner, Petya came home and told them his news. He said people had been collecting weapons at the Kremlin, and though Rostopchin's broadsheet had promised two or three days' warning, the order had already been given for everyone to go armed to the Three Hills tomorrow — there was going to be a big battle there.

The countess looked with timid horror at her son's eager, excited face. She realized that if she said a word about his not going to the battle (she knew how much he relished the thought), he would say something about men, honor, and the fatherland — something senseless, masculine, and unanswerable — and her plans would be ruined. So, hoping to arrange to leave before then and take Petya along as their protector and defender, she said nothing. After dinner, she took the count aside and, in tears, begged him to take her away — that very night if possible. With a woman's instinctive, loving cunning, she who until then had shown no alarm now said she would die of fright if they didn't leave that very night. Without pretending, she was now afraid of everything.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XIV
paragraphs: Madame Schoss, who had been visiting her daughter, increased the countess's fears still further by describing what she'd seen at a liquor shop on Myasnitsky Street. Returning by that street, she'd been unable to pass because of a drunken crowd rioting in front of the shop. She'd taken a cab and gone home by a side street, and the cabman told her the people were smashing open the barrels at the drink store, having been given orders to do so.

After dinner the whole Rostov household set to work with feverish haste packing and preparing for departure. The old count, suddenly leaping into action, kept rushing between the yard and the house, shouting confused instructions and making everyone even more flustered. Petya took charge in the yard. Sonya, overwhelmed by the count's contradictory orders, lost her bearings entirely. The servants ran noisily through the house and yard, shouting and arguing. Natasha, with the fierce determination she brought to everything, threw herself into the work too. At first her involvement was met with skepticism — everyone expected some prank and didn't want to obey her. But she resolutely and passionately demanded compliance, grew angry, nearly cried because they wouldn't listen, and finally made them trust her. Her first feat — which took enormous effort and established her authority — was the packing of the carpets. The count owned valuable Gobelin tapestries and Persian carpets. When Natasha started, two cases stood open in the ballroom — one nearly full of crockery, the other of carpets. There was also a great deal of china on the tables, with more being brought from the storeroom. A third case was needed, and servants had gone to fetch one.
"Sonya, wait — we'll fit everything into these," said Natasha.
"You can't, miss — we've already tried," said the butler's assistant.
"No, hold on, please."
And Natasha began rapidly taking out the paper-wrapped dishes and plates from the case.
"The dishes should go in here, among the carpets," she said.
"It would be a miracle if we could get the carpets alone into three cases," said the butler's assistant.

"Just wait, please!" And Natasha began quickly and deftly sorting things. "These aren't needed," she said, setting aside some Kiev-ware plates. "These, yes — these go among the carpets," she said, referring to the Saxony china.
"Don't, Natasha! Leave it — we'll manage!" Sonya urged reproachfully.
"What a young lady!" the major-domo remarked.

But Natasha refused to give in. She emptied everything out and started repacking from scratch, deciding that the cheaper Russian carpets and unnecessary crockery shouldn't be taken at all. When everything had been removed from the cases and repacking began, it turned out that with the less valuable items rejected, the important ones actually did fit into the two cases. Only the lid of the carpet case wouldn't close. A few more items could have been taken out, but Natasha insisted on doing it her way. She packed, repacked, pressed, enlisted the butler's assistant and Petya — whom she'd drafted into the operation — to lean on the lid, and pushed desperately herself.
"That's enough, Natasha," said Sonya. "I see you were right, but just take out the top one."
"I won't!" cried Natasha, holding back with one hand the hair that hung over her sweating face while pressing down the carpets with the other. "Press now, Petya! Press, Vasilich — push hard!"

The carpets yielded and the lid closed. Natasha clapped her hands and screamed with delight, and tears fell from her eyes. But this lasted only a moment. She immediately set to work again, and now they trusted her completely. The count wasn't even angry when told Natasha had countermanded one of his orders, and the servants now came to her to ask whether a cart was loaded enough and whether it could be roped up. Thanks to Natasha's direction, the work went swiftly — unnecessary things were left behind and the most valuable items packed as tightly as possible.
But however hard they all worked late into the night, they couldn't get everything packed. The countess had fallen asleep, and the count, putting off departure until the next morning, went to bed.
Sonya and Natasha slept in the sitting room without undressing.

That night another wounded man was brought down the Povarskaya, and Mavra Kuzminichna, standing at the gate, had him brought into the Rostovs' yard. She judged he must be a very important person. He was being carried in a carriage with a raised hood, completely covered by a traveling blanket. On the box beside the driver sat a dignified old attendant. A doctor and two soldiers followed in a cart.
"Please come in here. The family is leaving and the whole house will be empty," the old woman said to the attendant.
"Well, perhaps," he said with a sigh. "We don't expect to get him home alive. We have our own house in Moscow, but it's a long way from here and nobody's living in it."
"Please, do us the honor — there's plenty of everything in the master's house. Come in," said Mavra Kuzminichna. "Is he very ill?" she asked.
The attendant made a hopeless gesture.
"We don't expect to get him home. We'll have to ask the doctor."
And the old servant climbed down from the box and went to the cart.
"All right," said the doctor.
The old servant returned to the carriage, looked inside, shook his head sadly, told the driver to turn into the yard, and stopped beside Mavra Kuzminichna.
"Lord Jesus Christ!" she murmured.
She invited them to bring the wounded man inside.
"The family won't mind..." she said.
But they had to avoid carrying him upstairs, so they put him in the wing — in the room that had been Madame Schoss's.
This wounded man was Prince Andrew Bolkonsky.
